newsitem.title: USA: Gore, Kemp hurl acronyms, policy trivia in debate.
newsitem.headline: Gore, Kemp hurl acronyms, policy trivia in debate.

text.p: Democratic Vice President Al Gore and Republican rival Jack Kemp went into their debate on Wednesday as reputed "policy wonks" -- experts on the issues. They ended up coming across as wordy bookworms.

During the 90-minute televised debate, they threw out words that only specialists could understand, from "chlorofluorocarbon abatement," to "red-lining" and "green- lining," "entrepreneurial risk-taking" and "project XL ... at EPA."

"The single greatest problem, in our opinion, in the domestic economy is that this tax code, 83 years old, a relic of the Cold War and hot war, inflation and depression, 7.5 million words long, overtaxes capital, overtaxes working men and women and families. Clearly the Gordian Knot needs to be broken in one fell swoop."
Or this Kemp statement on foreign policy:

"We should have a foreign policy that is predicated upon trade, on spreading democracy, by giving people opportunities to trade freely with us and making sure that everybody recognises the rule of the ... the Golden Rule, to do unto others as you would have them do unto you. Diplomacy first, and don't bomb before breakfast."
Not to be outdone, Gore expounded on his speciality, the environment:

"We have been taking a new approach: protecting the environment but getting rid of unnecessary regulations. We're eliminating 16,000 pages of regulations. We've entered into a new project called Project XL -- this is at the EPA -- where we enter into a bargain with businesses. When they say, 'we'll exceed the standards,' we say, 'give the EPA a way to measure the progress and then throw away the rule book altogether.'"
Or this unexplained Gore reference to a "home testing kit" and the Food and Drug Administration:

"There was a story in the newspaper the other day about a home testing kit that the FDA had held up. That happened under a rule in the last administration. We said change that rule. It's being changed now. It's under consideration by the FDA right now and it will be changed. There are thousands of other examples."
And speaking of acronyms, Gore also regaled Americans about OSHA, which Washington insiders know as the Occupational Safety and Health Administration.
"We're taking a brand new approach to eliminate unnecessary regulations, unnecessary bureaucracies. We're re-inventing the way OSHA does its job. Some people would like to eliminate OSHA."
But it was Kemp who got himself into this tangle on taxes:

"Well, we have to have the type of economic prosperity that will allow us to generate the revenues to provide this technology. Ten percent of all the emissions, 10 percent of all the hydrocarbon emissions, oxides going into the air are caused by just 10 percent -- 100 percent of all the emissions are caused by 10 percent of the automobiles."
